newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania promises to reform industry at IMF urging.
newsitem.headline: Romania promises to reform industry at IMF urging.

text.p: Romania's government pledged on Thursday to shut down inefficient plants after the International Monetary Fund chided it for delaying an overhaul of loss-making industry.

At the end of a month-long IMF mission assessing market reforms, Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea said 17 factories -- oil refineries, machine plants and food processing facilities -- were being closed with 30,000 job losses.
"Supplies of energy, water, raw materials, transport -- all utilities -- are being cut to these 17 companies as we speak," Ciorbea told a news conference.
He said the plants would be shut as part of his centrist coalition's efforts to stem long-term losses to the state budget and secure fresh Western credits.
"The liquidation procedure can go on for months, but we cannot sit and wait for those companies to incur more and more losses," he said.

"Any single day we delay threatens the macro-stabilisation we have achieved. From this moment, the government, the trade unions and the population as a whole must pass the ultimate baptism of fire of structural reform."

The IMF's chief negotiator for Romania, Poul Thomsen, praised the results of reforms launched by the government since it took over last year after seven years of leftist rule. He pointed to lower inflation, a stable currency and increased foreign exchange reserves.

He said the government's budget, approved this week after revisions to take account of changed indicators and shortfalls in revenue, had done well to keep social programmes intact. But it had been slow to tackle restructuring in areas other than agriculture, he said.

"As far as structural reforms are concerned, we have to refocus efforts by picking out those enterprises which account for losses, accelerate privatisation and close down those that are unviable," Thomsen told Reuters.

"This has to happen here, now. And we have to be realistic about this. It means taking on the traditional strong vested interests -- the mining sector, the refining sector. The difficult problems are still ahead."

Thomsen said he would tell the IMF board, yet to decide whether to release the second of five $86 million credits, that "this remains a strong programme once the reform effort is refocused". Indicators, he said, remained "essentially the same with minor adjustments".
Government ministers have pledged to keep the deficit to 4.5 percent of gross domestic product as demanded by the IMF.

New figures announced by Ciorbea estimate monthly inflation of no more than two percent from now until year-end. Annual year-on-year inflation for 1997 is expected to be around 130 percent, above earlier estimates of 90 percent, after big rises in March and April.
Confusion has surrounded the government's plans to shut down inefficient industry since the publication earlier this year of several lists of plants earmarked for closure.
Ciorbea said the 17 plants, which ministers deemed unviable for privatisation, included three of Romania's 11 underused oil refineries.

Ministers have pledged to reduce Romania's vast annual refining capacity of 34 million tonnes by about two-thirds as part of plans to dismantle the National Oil Company and replace it with a more efficient operation.

Ciorbea said his government's biggest privatisation body would negotiate agreements with 40 international investment banks on privatising several dozen large Romanian firms. He said most of the more than 1,000 companies turned over to private hands this year were small and brought in low receipts.
